_comment: Guided tours for the Trainer hub. Two kinds, and the difference matters: "pages" are spoken tours (beats highlight element ids via .tour-glow, audio tour-<lang>-<page>-<n>.mp3 in trainer/audio/, built with scripts/site/build_trainer_tour.py) and "onboard" entries are text-only orientation, rendered without a player. A page belongs under "pages" only while its recorded words still match what the page says. The 6 Sep 2026 revision rewrote home, present, learn, plan, rollout, progress, pushback and the playbook index, and added first-session, so those live in "onboard"; their old mp3s stay on disk untouched and are simply no longer referenced. Moving a page back into "pages" means a new authorized audio pass — never re-point a page at a recording of older wording, and never edit a single beat of a page that still has audio, because audio is matched by beat index. The guide figure is never given a name.

index.title: First time here?
steps: Prepare one session first: try one card yourself, read one run sheet, rehearse ten minutes with a colleague.
The catalog, the planning tools and the rollout pages stay below, for when you need them.

first-session.title: How this page works
steps: Three steps, about an hour in total, and you are ready to run your first session.
Everything you need is linked here. Nothing else is required for a standard first run.

present.title: Choosing a format
steps: Pick by the slot you have: 30, 60 or 90 minutes. All three run from the same deck; the run sheet says which slides you use.
The 15-minute first look and the sales-cycle sprint are optional extras, not steps on the way.

selflearn.title: How to use these decks
steps: Nobody presents these. They are reference: look up the door your group asks about.
You do not have to read them before your first session.

plan.title: Planning in short
steps: Choose a prepared 30, 60 or 90 minute session. Its run sheet explains the slides, exercises and timing.
The tools below adapt a session to a specific group. They are optional.

weeks.title: The first four weeks
steps: Week one is your first session, prepared on the first-session page.
The weeks after that turn one session into a routine and a short note back.

progress.title: What to track
steps: Two things carry the story: how many people you reached, and how many produced a checked result on their own.
The seven-day follow-up gives you the second number.

resistance.title: Leadership says no time?
steps: Make the ask small: thirty minutes, or fifteen inside a meeting that already exists.
Bring something from their own team, not from the program: what people produced, and who used it again.

playbook.title: The playbook
steps: Four short chapters that hold what exists only here.
Chapter one goes with your first session; the rest is there when you need it.

faq.idle: Worried about the hard questions? Thirty seconds.
faq.done: Open the one you expect to hear. The answers are yours to use as they are.

beats.text: These are the objections you will actually hear, collected from the sales survey and the first trainings, roughly in the order they come up.
Every answer stands on the same two feet: the data rules are built into the lessons, and a person checks before anything reaches a customer. Say that early, not as a disclaimer at the end.

quiet.idle: Usage fading after the start? Thirty seconds.
quiet.done: Small and regular beats big and rare.

beats.text: Every rollout dips after the first weeks. Expect it, and treat it as maintenance, not failure.
Usage survives on rhythm: the link stays in the meeting notes, one card of the week, and one question, what did you try and what did it save.
And when it has gone quiet, restart small. A fifteen-minute refresher with one card, or a colleague showing their own win. Never answer a dip with a bigger training.

language.done: Translate the pages, and let the AI answer in your language.

beats.text: Everything here is written in English, but nobody has to wait for a translation. Your browser translates any page in one right-click, and it remembers your choice.

More importantly, the AI itself speaks your language. Write to Gemini and to the prepared Gems in your language and they answer in it, so coaching, negotiation practice and customer emails all happen locally.

One caveat worth saying in a session: the browser decides how it words a translated label, so a card can read slightly differently on your participants' screens than on your slide. Point at the position, and name the English original once.
